title: Chapter 9. Of the Several Subjects of Knowledge
paragraphs: KNOWLEDGE is of two kinds. One is knowledge of fact; the other is knowledge of the consequence of one affirmation to another. The first is nothing but sense and memory, and it is absolute knowledge — as when we see a fact being done, or remember it as done; this is the kind of knowledge required of a witness. The second is called science, and it is conditional — as when we know that if the figure shown is a circle, then any straight line through its centre divides it into two equal parts. This is the kind of knowledge required of a philosopher: that is, of anyone who claims to reason.

The record of knowledge of fact is called history. There are two sorts. One is natural history, which is the history of those facts, or effects of nature, that have no dependence on the will of man — such as the histories of metals, plants, animals, regions, and the like. The other is civil history, which is the history of the voluntary actions of men in commonwealths.

The records of science are the books that contain the demonstrations of the consequences of one affirmation to another; these are commonly called books of philosophy. They are of many sorts, according to the variety of the subject matter, and may be divided in the manner I have divided them in the table that follows.
I. Science, that is, knowledge of consequences; which is also called PHILOSOPHY
A. Consequences from the accidents (that is, the properties and qualities) of natural bodies; which is called NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
1. Consequences from the accidents common to all natural bodies; which are quantity and motion.
a. Consequences from indeterminate quantity and motion; which, being the principles or first foundation of philosophy, is called Philosophia Prima (First Philosophy)
a. Consequences from the qualities of transient bodies — those that sometimes appear and sometimes vanish
2) Consequences of the qualities from liquid bodies that fill the space between the stars — that is, the air, or the ethereal substance.
B. Consequences from the accidents of political bodies; which is called POLITICS, and CIVIL PHILOSOPHY
1. Of consequences from the founding of COMMONWEALTHS, to the rights and duties of the body politic, or sovereign.
2. Of consequences from that same founding, to the duty and right of the subjects.
